title: Urtica dioica
wiki_lead:
Urtica dioica, often known as common nettle, burn nettle, stinging nettle, nettle leaf, or just a nettle or stinger, is a herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Urticaceae. Originally native to Europe, much of temperate Asia and western North Africa, it is now found worldwide. 
The species is divided into six subspecies, five of which have many hollow stinging hairs called trichomes on the leaves and stems, which act like hypodermic needles, injecting histamine and other chemicals that produce a stinging sensation upon contact ("contact urticaria", a form of contact dermatitis).
The plant has a long history of use as a source for traditional medicine, food, tea, and textile raw material in ancient (such as Saxon) and modern societies.

Urtica dioica, often known as common nettle, burn nettle, stinging nettle, nettle leaf, or just a nettle or stinger, is a herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Urticaceae. Originally native to Europe, much of temperate Asia and western North Africa, it is now found worldwide. 
The species is divided into six subspecies, five of which have many hollow stinging hairs called trichomes on the leaves and stems, which act like hypodermic needles, injecting histamine and other chemicals that produce a stinging sensation upon contact ("contact urticaria", a form of contact dermatitis).
The plant has a long history of use as a source for traditional medicine, food, tea, and textile raw material in ancient (such as Saxon) and modern societies.


Description
Urtica dioica is a dioecious, herbaceous, and perennial plant. It grows to 0.9 to 2 metres (3 to 7 feet) tall in the summer and dying down to the ground in winter. It has widely spreading rhizomes and stolons, which are bright yellow, as are the roots. The soft, green leaves are around 8 cm long, ranging from 3 to 20 cm (1 to 6 in),  appearing in opposite pairs. The leaves have a strongly serrated margin, a cordate base, and an acuminate tip with a terminal leaf tooth longer than adjacent laterals. It bears small, greenish or brownish, numerous flowers in dense axillary inflorescences.
The leaves and stems are very hairy with non-stinging hairs, and in most subspecies, also bear many stinging hairs (trichomes or spicules), whose tips come off when touched, transforming the hair into a needle that can inject several chemicals causing a painful sting or paresthesia, giving the species its common names: stinging nettle, burn-nettle, burn-weed, or burn-hazel.


Taxonomy

Credit for the scientific naming of Urtica dioica is given to Carl Linnaeus, who published it in Species Plantarum in 1753. The taxonomy of Urtica species is confused, and sources are likely to use a variety of systematic names for these plants. Until 2014 there was broad consensus that the nettles native to the Americas, now classified as Urtica gracilis, were subspecies of U. dioica. However, in that year the paper "Weeding the Nettles II" was published in the journal Phytotaxa demonstrating the genetic distinctness of New World nettles. As of 2023 Plants of the World Online (POWO) recognises U. gracilis as a distinct species while the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service PLANTS database continues to list it as U. dioica subsp. gracilis, as does the Flora of North America.
As of 2023 POWO recognises 11 subspecies or varieties of U. dioica:

Urtica dioica subsp. afghanica Chrtek, from southwestern and central Asia, sometimes has stinging hairs or is sometimes hairless.
Urtica dioica subsp. dioica (European stinging nettle), from Europe, Asia, and northern Africa, has stinging hairs.
Urtica dioica subsp. gansuensis C.J.Chen, from eastern Asia (China), has stinging hairs.

grok_lead: Urtica dioica, commonly known as stinging nettle, is a rhizomatous perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the family Urticaceae, characterized by its erect stems and leaves armed with stinging trichomes that inject irritant chemicals upon contact, causing a burning sensation and skin rash. It typically grows 50â300 cm tall with square, wiry green stems and opposite, ovate to lanceolate leaves that are 6â20 cm long and 2â13 cm wide, featuring coarsely toothed margins and sparse to dense stinging hairs primarily on the undersides. The inconspicuous green to brownish flowers, arranged in drooping axillary racemes 3â7 cm long, are radially symmetrical with four sepals and are either staminate or pistillate, depending on the subspecies; the plant produces small, dry achene fruits 1â1.4 mm long. Native to Europe, temperate Asia, western North Africa, and parts of western North America, U. dioica has been widely introduced and naturalized across North America, including all U.S. states except Hawaii, and throughout Canada, often forming dense colonies in disturbed habitats. It thrives in moist, nutrient-rich soils such as those found in floodplains, forest edges, meadows, streambanks, ditches, and woodland clearings, preferring full sun to partial shade but intolerant of drought. Ecologically, it reproduces vegetatively via extensive rhizomes and sexually through wind-pollinated flowers from late spring to autumn, serving as a larval host for various butterflies including the painted lady ( Vanessa cardui) and red admiral ( Vanessa atalanta), while its rapid growth can make it a competitive weed in agricultural and natural areas. Beyond its notoriety for stinging, U. dioica holds significant ethnobotanical value, with leaves harvested young for culinary use in soups, teas, and as a nutritious vegetable rich in vitamins, minerals, and high-quality complete protein containing all essential amino acids (with protein comprising approximately 25â38% of dry weight and a balanced amino acid profile superior to many other leafy greens), after the stinging hairs are neutralized by cooking or drying. Traditionally employed in herbal medicine for its diuretic, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant propertiesâsupported by studies on its bioactive compounds like flavonoids and polyphenolsâit is used to treat conditions such as arthritis, urinary issues, and skin ailments, though clinical evidence remains limited. The plant's fibers have historical applications in textiles and cordage, and modern research explores its potential in phytoremediation and as a source of biofuel.
